newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine presidential "wannabes" put on show.
newsitem.headline: Philippine presidential "wannabes" put on show.

text.p: Tiger Bobby probably won the most laughs, the "honorary woman" claimed his best moment was passing a new Central Bank law and the only real woman on the stage hoped God would be the winner.

But most prominent at what organisers billed as the Presidential Derby '98 was a large name-card on the podium for the clear front-runner in the race to lead the Philippines into the next century -- but no sign of the man himself.
A year still to go, and the Philippines presidential race is already well underway.

On Thursday, five of the so-called "wannabes" for the country's highest post told a paying, and sometimes enthusiastic, audience in one of Manila's priciest hotels how they would bring greater prosperity to the largely-impoverished Philippines.
"We must go for a world class economy with a world class mentality," said Robert de Ocampo, warning of a dangerous national trait of settling for mediocrity.

As Finance Secretary and key figure in the reforms that have sparked rapid economic growth since President Fidel Ramos took office five years ago, de Ocampo could expect a warm reception from the audience, comprising much of Manila's elite.

Even the organisers referred to the event as a "show" and de Ocampo won laughs, and an occasional snigger, with his self-styled nickname "Tiger Bobby" -- a reference to champion golfer Tiger Woods and Philippine ambitions to become the next Asian tiger economy.

But in the end it was a mostly serious affair, strong on vision rather than substance, as hopefuls to become the third democratically elected president since the end of the Marcos dictatorship in 1986 fielded questions set by the Philippine alumni of the Harvard-Kennedy School of Government.

Asked for his best experience, Raul Roco, a hefty senator who likes to be called an "honourary woman" for his efforts to improve the lot of Filipinas, cited his success in pushing through a new Central Banking law.

Little room was given for controversy as each speaker echoed the other in promising to propel the Philippines -- with more food, jobs and better health and education -- into the 21st century as a country of substance and no longer as the "sick man of Asia."
"We are the only Christian country in Asia...God must win in Malacanang (the presidential palace)," said Gloria Arroyo, a former president's daughter and the only woman among the five.
An economist, she pledged that if she won her relatives would be barred from doing contracts with the government.

Edgardo Angara, a professor and a senator, repeatedly stressed the need for better education while House Speaker Jose de Venecia recalled the many successes of his career. Neither is seen as a strong contender.
Notably absent from the "derby" was vice-president Joseph Estrada, who on Wednesday resigned from his Cabinet position to start in earnest for the campaign.

The former action-hero film star, who says his days of womanising and heavy drinking are over, is generally seen as the man to beat, commanding huge popularity among the masses for whom his macho film image still lingers.
The candidate, for the moment, seen as having one of the best chances of beating Estrada, Defence Minister Renato de Villa, also decided not to come.
De Villa's standing is high because of the suggestion that President Ramos might name him as his preferred successor when his six-year term ends next year.
